name: Nineteen Eighty-Four (1984)
blurb: George Orwell's novel of a man who rebels against an all-seeing totalitarian state
title: 1984 Summary: Plot, Characters and Ending Explained
description: 1984 by George Orwell summary: Winston, Julia, O'Brien and Big Brother, what happens in each of the three parts, the ending explained, and the key themes.
h1: Nineteen Eighty-Four (1984): Summary, Characters and Ending Explained
answer: Nineteen Eighty-Four is a novel by the British writer George Orwell, published on 8 June 1949. It is set in London, now the capital of Airstrip One, a province of the superstate Oceania, ruled by a single Party whose leader, Big Brother, watches everyone through telescreens. Winston Smith, a low-ranking Party member whose job is rewriting old newspapers, secretly hates the regime. The novel follows his private rebellion against a state that controls not only what people do but what they are allowed to think and remember.

body: Part One: Winston's doubts. On a cold April day in 1984, Winston returns to his flat in Victory Mansions and begins a diary, a crime that could cost him his life. Oceania is permanently at war with one of the other two superstates, Eurasia or Eastasia, and the Party changes the enemy whenever it suits it. At the Ministry of Truth, Winston alters old news reports and records so that the past always agrees with what the Party says now; people the Party has vaporised are erased from every document. During the daily Two Minutes Hate against Goldstein, he notices O'Brien, whom he suspects of sharing his doubts, and Julia, whom he fears is a spy. Syme explains that Newspeak is designed to make rebellious thought impossible, and Winston predicts that Syme will disappear. Winston wanders among the proles, the poor majority the Party barely watches, and buys the diary and later a glass paperweight from Mr Charrington's shop.

Part Two: the affair and the book. Julia slips Winston a note saying she loves him. They meet secretly in the countryside and become lovers; for Julia, rebellion is about enjoying life and breaking rules without being caught. They rent the room above Mr Charrington's shop, which seems to have no telescreen, and meet there for weeks. Syme vanishes as Winston predicted. O'Brien invites Winston to his flat, switches off his telescreen and tells Winston and Julia that the Brotherhood is real. They swear to do anything for it, short of separating from each other. O'Brien arranges for Winston to receive Goldstein's forbidden book, which explains how the Party keeps the world divided and at war to stay in power. While Winston reads it aloud to Julia in their room, a voice speaks from a telescreen hidden behind a picture. Thought Police burst in, and Mr Charrington is revealed as one of them.

Part Three: the Ministry of Love. Winston is held without daylight in the Ministry of Love, where he sees other prisoners, including Parsons, who was denounced by his own daughter. O'Brien is his interrogator; he admits that he was never a rebel and that the book was written partly by him. Over months of beatings and electric shocks, O'Brien teaches Winston that reality is whatever the Party says it is, holding up four fingers until Winston truly sees five. O'Brien explains that the Party seeks power purely for its own sake. Winston confesses to everything and accepts every lie, but still privately loves Julia and hates Big Brother. So he is taken to Room 101, which holds each prisoner's worst fear. For Winston it is rats: a cage of starving rats is fixed to his face, and he screams for them to be put on Julia instead.

Winston is released. He spends his days drinking gin at the Chestnut Tree Café, where he once saw three disgraced Party men who were later arrested again. He meets Julia by chance; both admit they betrayed each other, and they feel nothing. In the café, news arrives of a great Oceanian victory in Africa. Winston weeps with gratitude, gazing at Big Brother's face, and the novel ends with the statement that he loves Big Brother. He expects that one day he will be shot.

Most readers take the ending as total defeat: the Party has not only punished Winston but changed what he feels, which is its stated aim. A second, debated reading looks at the appendix, The Principles of Newspeak, which is written in standard English and refers to Newspeak in the past tense, as if from a time after the Party; some critics read this as a sign that the regime eventually fell. Orwell, who was seriously ill with tuberculosis while finishing the book and died in January 1950, gave no fuller explanation of the appendix. The novel is widely read as a warning about totalitarianism in any form, drawing on Stalin's Soviet Union and Nazi Germany, rather than as a prediction of a particular year.

ul: Totalitarianism: the Party controls work, love, language and memory, and wants obedience from the inside, not just outward conformity.
Surveillance: telescreens, informers and the Thought Police mean no one can be sure of privacy, even in their own home.
Control of truth and history: Winston's job shows how a state that controls records can make the past whatever it needs, and O'Brien demands that he accept that two and two make five.
Language and thought: Newspeak cuts down the vocabulary so that ideas such as freedom can no longer be expressed, and so no longer thought.
Doublethink and slogans: the Party teaches people to hold contradictory beliefs at once, summed up in its slogans "War is peace. Freedom is slavery. Ignorance is strength."
Length: three parts plus an appendix, usually around 300–330 pages.
Background: Orwell wrote it in the late 1940s, partly on the Scottish island of Jura; terms from it, such as Big Brother, thoughtcrime, doublethink and Room 101, are now common in English.
Adaptations: film versions appeared in 1956 and in 1984, the latter starring John Hurt as Winston.
Content: torture described in detail, psychological cruelty and a bleak ending.

What teachers usually ask about: how the Party keeps power, Winston's job at the Ministry of Truth, the role of Newspeak, why O'Brien wants belief and not just obedience, and what the ending and the appendix mean.

check.why: Winston alters past newspapers and documents so they match whatever the Party says now.

check.why: The kindly shopkeeper who rented Winston and Julia their room is revealed as an agent when they are arrested.

options: A mirror showing his ruined body
check.why: Rats are Winston's worst fear, and the threat makes him betray Julia.

faq.a: It stands for the Party's power over truth itself. O'Brien wants Winston to believe that two and two make five if the Party says so, and after his release Winston traces the sum in the dust on a café table, showing that he has given in.

faq.q: Is Big Brother a real person?
faq.a: The novel never says. Winston asks O'Brien whether Big Brother exists in the way he himself does, and O'Brien answers only that Big Brother exists and will never die, as the embodiment of the Party. Goldstein's existence is just as uncertain.

It is the year in which the story is set, though Winston himself is not sure it really is 1984, since the Party controls all records. Orwell finished the novel in 1948, and the working title was The Last Man in Europe.
